 Order

The present petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has been filed assailing the order dated 07.09.2018 passed in Criminal Revision No.18/2018 by Additional Sessions Judge/Special Judge, Harda arising out of order dated 09.02.2018 passed in R.C.T.
No.1411/2017 by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Harda whereby the the application filed by the applicant under Section 239 of the Cr.P.C. has been rejected.
2.
The case of the applicant is that the applicant is a resident of Gujarat and is doing business as a grain merchant.

One Hemant Kumar Jain, proprietor of Jain Industries, Harda lodged an FIR to the effect that he being a grain merchant has supplied 300 quintals of wheat amounting to Rs.6,35,700/- on 12.04.2017 and 216 quintals of wheat amounting to Rs.4,35,7509/- on 18.04.2017 through Brokers Rajkumar Jain having Firm "Jain Canvassers" and Ketan having firm "Jai Ambe Corporation" of NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:41918 2 MCRC-5107-2019 Ahmedabad to Umia Trading Company Ahmedabad, Gujarat and Futura Enterprises, Ahmedabad,
Gujarat respectively.
It is alleged that the complainant has not received the amount of sale consideration, as such the purchasers and brokers have committed criminal breach of trust.
On the basis of the FIR, a criminal case was registered for an offence punishable under Section 406 of the IPC and was investigated.
During the course of investigation, statements of witnesses were recorded under Section 161 of the Cr.P.C.

After arresting the accused persons, their memorandum have been Mahesh Thakkar vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 13 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/128641439/
1 recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.

sentences.text: The memorandum of the applicant has also been recorded, wherein, he has clearly stated that he has purchased wheat from Futura Company from 20.03.2017 till 01.04.2017 amounting to Rs.34,69,198/- for which the payments have been made through RTGS and thereafter he has not made any purchase through Umia Trading Company or Futura Trading Company.
None of the co-accused persons have given any statement against the applicant.
There is no verbatim in the statements which have been recorded under Section 161 of the Cr.P.C. to show the involvement of applicant in commission of offence.

Therefore, he has filed an application under Section 239 of the Cr.P.C. asking for discharge as there was no material against him in the documents which have been collected by the Police authorities in terms of Section 173 of the Cr.P.C.
The said application has been rejected vide order dated 09.02.2018 on the ground that the same is a matter of evidence.
Thereafter, a revision has been preferred, the same stood dismissed on 07.09.2018.

3. Challenge to both the orders have been made on the grounds that NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2024:MPHC-JBP:41918 3 MCRC-5107-2019 there is no material in the entire charge-sheet, which has been filed by the police authorities showing involvement of the present applicant in commission of the offence.
Even the statements of other co-accused recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act does not implicate the present applicant.

He has categorically stated in his memorandum that the purchase of wheat from Futura Company was between 20.03.2017 till 01.04.2017 and thereafter no purchase has been made through Umia Trading Company or Futura Trading Company.
The amount towards the purchase has already been paid through RTGS.

He has drawn attention of this Court to the FIR, which has been registered on the basis of complaint made by the complainant and argued that from the perusal of the FIR it is apparently clear that there is nothing on record against the present applicant.
No involvement of the present applicant is reflected if the case of the complainant and the documents presented by the police authorities are considered as it is.

Under these circumstances, the case of the applicant is squarely covered in terms of the exceptions carved out by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of State of Haryana Vs. Bhajanlal reported in 1992 Suppl. SCC 335 as well as the recent judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Niharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Maharashtra and others reported in 2021 SCC OnLine 315.

It is submitted that the trial Court as well as the revisional Court has rightly recorded the fact that the contentions raised by the applicant are the matter of evidence,
At this stage it cannot be said that whether the involvement of the applicant is reflected or not.
Even otherwise, he has already been enlarged on bail, therefore, no prejudice will be caused to him if the entire trial is being faced.
There are some allegations with respect to transaction on sale-purchase of wheat during the intervening period.
He has prayed for dismissal of the petition.

sentences.text: Heard learned counsels for the parties and perused the record.

6. The FIR which has been lodged on 01.05.2017 is taken as it is then also the entire allegation is made against Jain Canvassers, through broker Rajkumar Jain and Jai Ambe Corporation through broker Ketan.
The date of transactions and the bills which have been mentioned in the FIR are also not matching with the statement recorded under Section 27 of the Evidence Act of the present applicant.
The FIR does not reflect the involvement of the applicant in any manner.

Even the complaint which has been made to the police authorities dated 01.05.2017 by the complainant i.e.
Hemant Kumar Jain i.e. proprietor of Jain Industries does not reflect the involvement of the present applicant.

The bill dated 12.04.2017, which has been produced bearing No.3942 showing the purchase of 300 quintals of wheat amounting to Rs.6,35,700/- from Jai Ambe Corporation and bill dated 18.04.2017 showing purchase of wheat of 216 quintals amounting to Rs.4,53,816/- from Futura Enterprises, Ahmedabad, Gujarat and further NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2024:MPHC-JBP:41918 5 MCRC-5107-2019 purchase of wheat of 210 quintals on 21.04.2017 amounting to Rs.4,35,750/- but the entire complaint does not reflect the involvement of the present applicant.
The present applicant is Mahesh Thakker and his name has not been shown either by the complainant or by any of the co-accused in the matter.
Counsel appearing for the State has failed to point out the involvement of the present applicant in the commission of offence.
He could not point out any document to show that the applicant is involved for commission of offence alleged in the complaint.

The learned trial Court as well as the revisional Court has failed to consider the aforesaid aspect of the matter and the only ground of consideration was that the same being a matter of evidence has rejected the application for discharge.
The fact remains that once a prima facie case is not made out against the applicant then he should not be roped up and forced to face a criminal trial.
7. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bhajanlal (supra) has laid down the principles for quashing of the proceeding.
The relevant observations of the Supreme Court are as follows:-

The core of the above sections namely 156, 157 and 159 of the Code is that if a police officer has reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence, he must either proceed with the investigation or cause an investigation to be proceeded with by his subordinate; that in a case where the police officer sees no sufficient ground for investigation, he can dispense with the investigation altogether; that the field of investigation of any cognizable offence is exclusively within the domain of the investigating agencies over which the courts cannot have control and have no power to stifle or impinge upon the proceedings in the investigation so long as the investigation proceeds in compliance with the provisions relating to investigation and that it is only in a case wherein a police officer decides not to investigate an offence,
the concerned Magistrate can intervene and either direct an investigation or in the alternative, if he thinks fit, he himself can, at once proceed or depute any Magistrate subordinate to him to proceed to hold a preliminary inquiry into or otherwise to dispose of the case in the manner provided in the Code.

sentences.text:
In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised.
(1) Where the allegations made in the first information report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.
(2) Where the allegations in the first information report and other materials, if any,
accompanying the FIR do not disclose a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code.

(3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused.

(4) Where, the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted by a police officer without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code.

(5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

(6)
Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party.

(7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal grudge.

8. The Hon'ble Supreme Court recently in the case of Niharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (supra) have framed certain guidelines for consideration of cases for quashment of FIR especially in paragraph 80, which reads as under :-
"80.

sentences.text: Therefore, when the investigation by the police is in progress, the court should not go into the merits of the allegations in the FIR.
Police must be permitted to complete the investigation.
It would be premature to pronounce the conclusion based on hazy facts that the complaint/FIR does not deserve to be investigated or that it amounts to abuse of process of law.

After investigation, if the investigating officer finds that there is no substance in the application made by the complainant, the investigating officer may file an appropriate report/summary before the learned Magistrate which may be considered by the learned Magistrate in accordance with the known procedure;
xiii) The power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is very wide, but conferment of wide power requires the court to be more cautious.
It casts an onerous and more diligent duty on the court;

xiv) However, at the same time, the court, if it thinks fit, regard being had to the parameters of quashing and the self-restraint imposed by law, more particularly the parameters laid down by this Court in the cases of R.P. Kapur (supra) and Bhajan Lal (supra), has the jurisdiction to quash the FIR/complaint;
xv) When a prayer for quashing the FIR is made by the alleged accused and the court when it exercises the power under Section 482 Cr.P.C., only has to consider whether the allegations in the FIR disclose commission of a cognizable offence or not.

The court is not required to consider on merits whether or not the merits of the allegations make out a cognizable offence and the court has to permit the investigating agency/police to investigate the allegations in the FIR;
xvi) The aforesaid parameters would be applicable and/or the aforesaid aspects are required to be considered by the High Court while passing an interim order in a quashing petition in exercise of powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and/or under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

However,
an interim order of stay of investigation during the pendency of the quashing petition can be passed with circumspection.
Such an interim order should not require to be passed routinely, casually and/or mechanically.

Normally, when the investigation is in progress and the facts are hazy and the entire evidence/material is not before the High Court, the High Court should restrain itself from passing the interim order of not to arrest or ''no coercive steps to be adopted and the accused should be relegated to apply for anticipatory bail under Section 438, Cr.P.C. before the competent court.

The High Court shall not and as such is not justified in passing the order of not to arrest and/or no Mahesh Thakkar vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 13 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/128641439/
6 coercive steps either during the investigation or till the investigation is completed and/or till the final report/charge NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:41918 9 MCRC-5107-2019 sheet is filed under Section 173 Cr.P.C., while dismissing/disposing of the quashing petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and/or under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

sentences.text: xvii) Even in a case where the High Court is prima facie of the opinion that an exceptional case is made out for grant of interim stay of further investigation, after considering the broad parameters while exercising the powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. and/or under Article 226 of the Constitution of India referred to hereinabove, the High Court has to give brief reasons why such an interim order is warranted and/or is required to be passed so that it can demonstrate the application of mind by the Court and the higher forum can consider what was weighed with the High Court while passing such an interim order.

xviii) Whenever an interim order is passed by the High Court of no coercive steps to be adopted within the aforesaid parameters, the High Court must clarify what does it mean by "no coercive steps to be adopted as the term" no coercive steps to be adopted can be said to be too vague and/or broad which can be misunderstood and/or misapplied."
9. In view of the forgoing discussions and the well settled propositions of law on the subject, the case of the applicant fall under the parameters for quashing as carved out in the aforesaid cases.

This Court is conscious about the fact regarding quashment of criminal proceedings in petition under Section 482, Cr.P.C., but the fact remains that if there is no material with the prosecution agency against the accused/applicant then he should not be unnecessarily forced to face a criminal prosecution.
The same will be amounting to abuse of the process of law in the hands of the prosecution as well as the complainant and unnecessary harassment to the accused/applicant.

10. Under these circumstances, the order dated 09.02.2018 passed by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Harda and the order dated 07.09.2018 passed by Additional Sessions Judge/Special Judge, Harda are unsustainable and are hereby set aside.
The application filed by the applicant under Section 239 of the Cr.P.C. is hereby allowed.

The applicant is discharged from NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2024:MPHC-JBP:41918 10 MCRC-5107-2019 criminal proceedings in FIR bearing Crime No.412 of 2018 for the offence under Sections 406, 420 and 34 of the IPC.
11.
Accordingly, the petition stands allowed.
